claims.text: Moderate thermal annealing induces a moderate degree of grain-boundary segregation in multiphase high-entropy alloys.
Moderate thermal annealing causes in-situ formation of metastable secondary phases.
Metastable secondary phases formed near grain boundaries undergo stress-induced transformation under applied load.
Stress-induced transformation of the secondary phases enhances toughness through transformation toughening.
Excessive annealing produces nanoclusters at grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary segregation weakens intergranular cohesion and can initiate decohesion.
Grain-boundary nanoclustering initiates decohesion or cavitation.
Varying annealing temperature and dwell time controls grain-boundary segregation and secondary-phase formation.
The relevant structural mediators are grain-boundary composition and the size and spatial distribution of in-situ precipitates.
An optimal annealing window will produce greater fracture strain and energy absorption than the as-cast or as-sintered baseline.
More severe annealing will reduce toughness through grain-boundary embrittlement.
Elemental segregation to grain boundaries can account for temperature-induced ductility loss in equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni.
Preexisting precipitates can divert rapidly segregating elements away from grain boundaries and thereby avoid intermediate-temperature ductility loss.
The baseline has relatively homogeneous grain-boundary chemistry and no engineered secondary precipitates.
The hypothesis should apply mainly to multiphase or heterogeneous HEAs and may not apply to single-phase HEAs.
The hypothesis may not apply when environmental effects such as oxidation dominate failure.
Failure to observe greater toughness after moderate annealing than after both baseline and severe annealing would falsify the proposed nonmonotonic mechanism.
